- When sentiment is high (≥0.7) and forecast shows a sharp upward spike, reduce the peak by 5–10% to avoid overshoot.  
- If sentiment is low (≤0.3) and forecast is rising, cap the increase at 2–3% above recent mean to avoid overreaction.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if the last 3–5 days show strong mean reversion (price dropping after spike), model should not overcorrect upward.  
- When sentiment is volatile (alternating 0.2–0.8), avoid extrapolating trend; use 2–3 day moving average for smoothing.  
- If true outcome exceeds forecast by >5% in 3 consecutive days, adjust next forecast downward by 1–2% to reflect momentum correction.  
- For forecasts with high variance in early days (e.g., first 5–7 days), apply a 1–2% downward bias if sentiment is neutral or negative.  
- If sentiment is consistently above 0.6 and price is trending up, reduce forecast slope slightly to avoid overestimating momentum.  
- If forecast is below true outcome by >3% for 3+ days, consider a 1–2% upward bias in next forecast to reflect lagged sentiment effect.
